title: The Commutative Tri-Modal Vault: Memory That Reasons
subtitle: Markdown notes, a fact graph and a vector space kept consistent: bridges, gardening, contradiction-aware retrieval and memory you can replay
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A beginner-friendly course on the Commutative Tri-Modal Vault (CTMV), a design for personal knowledge bases and AI memory that answers four failures: related ideas that never meet, collections that decay, old and new facts that both come back, and memory locked to one model. In 13 chapters you learn the three views of one vault (V markdown files, G facts and rules with proofs, M vectors), the commuting square and its error delta, cross-domain bridges, gap and contradiction gardening, metric warping, multi-hop retrieval that drops replaced notes and flags disputes, and replayable, model-agnostic memory. Five hands-on labs run in the app, offline, on real components: the Jade Agent Kit's SQLite with sqlite-vec and file system, and the Jade Vault's Datalog reasoner (jade-kg); only the text embedder is a small toy so results repeat. A few short Python labs run on the app's MicroPython. There are 26 numbered figures, numbered tables, a recap, a memory trick, an expanded ELI5 and a concept map in every chapter, a cheat sheet in the sandbox and a final exam. Credits: the CTMV concept follows the description supplied by the course requester; the text and code here are original. Labs use Jade Agent Kit (MIT), Jade Vault jade-kg (MIT), SQLite (public domain) and sqlite-vec by Alex Garcia (MIT or Apache-2.0). CTMV is a design to understand and test, not a proven product.

summary: CTMV keeps every note in three forms. V is the vault: plain markdown files. G is the graph: facts and rules that can be checked. M is the manifold: a vector for each note, so you can ask which notes are near each other.

V is the truth; G and M are built from it and can be rebuilt at any time. This is what makes the system inspectable. Each view is strong where another is weak, so the combination can do things none of them can alone.
The word commutative in the name is a promise about consistency, which chapter 6 explains with a diagram.

chapters.title: V: the markdown vault
summary: The vault is a folder of markdown files. A note has a heading, a line of tags, some prose, and optionally claim lines and links to other notes. Plain text means you can read it, back it up, search it with any tool and keep it for decades.

For the machine to reason about a note, the course uses one simple convention: a line that starts with a dash and has exactly three words is a claim, in the order subject, relation, object. Links are written in double square brackets.
Writes are atomic: write a temporary file, then rename it over the note. Then a power cut can never leave half a note.

chapters.title: G: facts, rules and proofs

maps.title: The graph
links: Open world | means | Unknown is allowed

summary: G is a small logic engine. Every claim line becomes a fact. Rules say what follows from facts, for example that a cause of a cause is also a cause further along.
Constraints say what must never happen, for example that the same thing may not both cause and prevent the same outcome.
The engine in the labs is the Jade Vault's knowledge reasoner, written in Rust and run as WebAssembly.
It speaks a Datalog-style language, answers questions with variables, verifies claims, and shows a proof listing every fact and rule it used.
It is an open world: if nothing is known, the answer is unknown, not false. This is the opposite of a database that treats missing as no.

A pattern that must never match; any match is a contradiction.
A small logic language with facts, rules and variables that begin with capitals.

ELI5. A very careful librarian. You tell her two facts, and ask if one leads to the other. She does not guess. She points to your two facts and the rule that joins them, or says she does not know.
Now the real words. G turns claim lines into facts. Rules derive more facts, constraints catch contradictions, and answers are proven, contradicted or unknown, with a proof.

Here is the idea in a story. You tell a very careful librarian: retry storms cause overload, and overload causes outage. You then ask, does a retry storm lead to an outage? The librarian does not guess. She points to your two statements and the rule that chains them. (See Figure 4.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.1. From a claim line to an answer that shows its proof.

lesson.code:
% a rule: a chain of causes
leads_to(X, Y) :- claim(N, X, causes, Y).
leads_to(X, Z) :- claim(N, X, causes, Y), leads_to(Y, Z).

% a constraint: a thing must not both cause and prevent the same outcome
! cause_and_prevent: claim(N1, X, causes, Y), claim(N2, X, prevents, Y).

items: Capital letters are variables, which stand for anything. The first rule says that any claim of the form X causes Y means X leads to Y. The second says if X causes Y and Y leads to Z, then X leads to Z.

summary: M gives every note a point in a space, a list of numbers called a vector. Notes with similar meaning should end up near each other, so you can ask for the nearest neighbours of a note or of a question. This is what vector databases do.
In real use an embedding model turns text into the numbers. In the labs, a small hashing function does it, so everything runs offline and gives the same numbers every time.
It is crude: it mostly notices shared words and word parts, not deep meaning.

The labs store vectors in SQLite using the sqlite-vec extension, from the Jade Agent Kit, and ask it for the nearest ones. Distance here is cosine distance: zero means the same direction, bigger means further apart.

chapters.title: The commuting square and the error δ

maps.title: Commutation
links: V | goes to G by | Extract pi
V | goes to M by | Embed phi
G | goes to M by | Warp f

summary: There are two ways to get from a note to a place in the manifold. One goes straight: embed the text, which is φ.
The other goes through logic: extract facts, which is π, and then use them to warp and anchor the geometry, which is f. If the two routes agree, the picture commutes.
The formula f∘π(v) ≅ φ(v) says that going through the facts lands near going straight. The error δ(v) measures how far apart the two routes end up for a note v.

In practice, no model is perfect, so δ is never zero everywhere. That is useful. Where the routes disagree, something interesting is happening: a hidden connection, a misleading resemblance, or a fact nobody wrote down.

glossary.def: The map from V to G: from text to facts.
The map from V to M: from text to a vector.
The map from G into M: using facts to adjust distances and positions.
Different routes to the same place give the same result.
The commutativity error: how much the two routes disagree for a note.

keyPoints: Two routes: embed directly, or extract facts and warp.
The square commutes if both routes meet.
δ measures disagreement per note.
High δ is a clue, not necessarily an error.

chapters.title: Failure three, part two: contradiction-aware multi-hop retrieval
summary: Retrieval for an AI helper should not return only the notes nearest to the question. It should return the right small set: the best match, the notes that explain it, and a warning where notes disagree. CTMV does this in four steps.

practice.intro: Write fingerprint(facts). facts is a list of strings. Sort them, join them with a newline, and return a 32-bit FNV-1a hash of the text as 8 lowercase hex digits. Start from 2166136261 and for each character: xor with its character code, multiply by 16777619, and keep the lowest 32 bits (and with 4294967295).
practice.hint: The order of the facts must not matter, so sort first.
practice.solution:
def fingerprint(facts):
    text = "\n".join(sorted(facts))
    h = 2166136261
    for ch in text:
        h = h ^ ord(ch)
        h = (h * 16777619) & 4294967295
    s = "%x" % h
    return "0" * (8 - len(s)) + s

summary: Artificial curiosity rewards compression progress, not surprise. A good hypothesis makes the vault shorter to describe, and a leap is such a hypothesis checked by the reasoner.

Creativity combines known patterns into new ones. In tests, a language model found cross-field bridges with 0.99 precision on clear notes, and a small tree-search agent found a law outside its library only when it could invent.

glossary.def: How much shorter the description of your data became after learning something.
Schmidhuber's idea: reward the agent for compression progress.
A hypothesis chosen because it would compress the vault, then checked by the reasoner.
Many hypotheses weighted by how simple they are and how well they predicted.
Plan by simulating many futures and favouring the good ones.
Hutter's idealised agent that plans over every simple world; only approximations can run.

keyPoints: Be curious about what you can learn, not what surprises you.
A leap is a hypothesis that shortens the description, checked by the reasoner.
Invention combines known patterns and pays a complexity cost.
Curiosity matters most when your model class is wrong.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Building it for real, and what to test next:
• The labs use Jade Agent Kit, jade-kg and sqlite-vec.
• A real embedder and a claim proposer are the missing parts.
• CozoDB could host both G and M in one place.
• A design is not a result; measure it.

ELI5. A child builds towers from blocks. Each time a new idea makes the tower simpler to describe, she gets a little happy. A pile of random blocks is exciting to look at but gives no such feeling, so she does not keep staring at it.
Now the real words. Artificial curiosity rewards compression progress. A hypothesis that makes the vault shorter to describe is worth testing. Noise surprises you but teaches nothing.

A leap is such a hypothesis chosen by that score and checked by the reasoner. Creativity combines known patterns into new ones, and a small agent can do science by planning experiments, being curious, inventing and predicting.
Try it. In Lab 5, ask which hypothesis compresses your notes most, take the leap, then add a filler note and see it score below zero.
If you remember one thing: Be curious about what you can learn, not about what only surprises you.
A knowledge base can find a bridge by looking, but a person often finds it by a hunch: this swing is like that feedback loop. Can a machine have such a hunch in a way we can test?

Here we try three ways: a curiosity score inside the vault, a language model asked to find shared mechanisms, and a small agent that does science in a simulated world. (See Figure 13.1 below.) (See Table 13.1 below.)

items: Noise earns nothing. A filler note about a weekly standup is surprising next to the rest of the vault, but no pattern predicts it, so every hypothesis about it scores minus one. Lab 5 shows both cases with the real reasoner.

The first test used embeddings alone. With patterns labelled in two or three domains and the domain part of each vector removed, the progress score labelled the other domains with precision 0.93 on templated notes and 0.53 on rewritten notes, against 0.11 to 0.19 for a plain one-shot tagger.
It ranks well but is not a labeller. Inventing a brand-new pattern from embeddings alone failed: the groups were barely purer than random.

The second test asked a language model, gemma4:31b, to read 45 notes without any pattern list and group notes that share a mechanism across fields. In 60 test vaults it found 1804 of 1812 planted bridges with precision 0.99, and did not group the false friends.
These planted analogies are written clearly and real notes will be harder, so treat it as a promising result, not a promise. (See Figure 13.2 below.) (See Table 13.2 below.)

items: In the simulation the agent studies a hidden system. If the law is one it knows, the planner needs one experiment and curiosity adds nothing, because a Bayesian planner already values information.
If the law is a new combination, such as logistic growth, a confident planner stops after about 1.4 experiments and is right a third of the time.

The curious one keeps going, sees that the data do not compress, invents, and is right 85 to 90 percent of the time. Creativity finds the law, curiosity keeps the search alive. (See Table 13.3 below.)

The limits matter. The world is small and hand-built, the inventions come from a fixed grammar, the planner is a rough approximation of AIXI, and the language-model test used clear notes. The code and numbers are in the benchmark report. (See Table 13.4 below.)

practice.title: Score a hypothesis
practice.intro: Write progress(stated, derived, label_cost). stated is the list of claims a note already makes; derived is the list of claims the reasoner derives once the hypothesis is added. Return how many stated claims are also derived, minus label_cost.
practice.hint: Count the stated claims that also appear in derived.
practice.solution:
def progress(stated, derived, label_cost):
    return len([c for c in stated if c in derived]) - label_cost

practice.title: Information gain in bits
practice.intro: Write info_gain(prior, likelihoods). Both are lists of the same length. Multiply each prior by its likelihood, divide by the total to get the posterior, and return the sum over hypotheses of posterior times log base 2 of posterior over prior, rounded to 3 decimals. Skip hypotheses whose posterior is 0.
practice.hint: Bayes update, then the Kullback-Leibler divergence in bits.
